The Varna Salt Cooperative was founded in 1911 by eleven families who worked the shallow lagoons south of the harbour. For the first decade they sold coarse grey salt to fish-curers along the coast, carrying it in flat-bottomed boats that could cross the lagoon at low water. In 1924 a storm breached the outer dyke and flooded half of the evaporation pans with fresh water; three seasons of production were lost, and six of the founding families left for the city. The remaining members borrowed money from a grain merchant, rebuilt the dyke with stone instead of packed clay, and switched from grey salt to a finer white salt that could be sold to bakeries. By 1935 the cooperative employed forty workers during the summer harvest and had bought a small steam pump. The pump allowed them to move brine between pans in a fixed sequence, which raised the yield per hectare by roughly a third. During the war the harbour was closed and the salt was moved inland by cart. After 1950 the cooperative slowly declined: refrigeration reduced demand from fish-curers, and a large industrial plant opened eighty kilometres to the north. The last harvest took place in 1971. Today the pans are a bird reserve, and the old pump house is a small museum.

Based only on the text above: why did the cooperative switch from grey salt to white salt, and what made that possible?

Mira kept a notebook of every bridge she crossed during a month of walking along the river. On the first day she counted a rope footbridge near the source, swaying above a narrow gorge. Two days later she reached a stone arch with seven spans, built, according to a plaque, by monks who charged a toll in candles. In the market town she crossed an iron bridge painted green, then a concrete road bridge that carried lorries toward the motorway. Further down the valley the river widened and the bridges became rarer; for four days she saw only a ferry, a wooden raft pulled along a cable by an old man who refused payment and asked instead for news from upstream. Near the estuary she found a railway viaduct, so tall that swallows nested under its deck, and finally a swing bridge that opened twice a day to let fishing boats reach the sea. On the last page of the notebook she wrote that the bridges had told her the history of the valley better than any book: who travelled, what they carried, and who paid for the crossing.

Summarise the text above in three sentences, and name the bridge Mira found most unusual.
